summary: A liaison statement from an ITU-T working party to the IETF and ISOC about ENUM, the idea of mapping telephone numbers to Internet addresses through DNS. It records understandings from a 2000 meeting in Berlin. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: One group of experts wrote a letter to another group to share what they had agreed about turning phone numbers into Internet names.

questions: what is an itu liaison to the ietf
subtitle: A letter from an ITU-T working party on who supplies telephone-number data for DNS-based ENUM.

tldr.problem: ENUM puts telephone (E.164) numbers into the DNS under e164.arpa, but the numbers are handed out by telephone-numbering bodies, not by DNS operators. Someone had to say who supplies which data.
tldr.mechanism: A working party of the ITU-T split the e164.arpa name into zones and recorded who is responsible for each: the ITU for country codes, member states for national geographic numbers, and the assigned entity for network and group codes.
tldr.outcome: The memo is an informational record of the understandings reached at a 2000 meeting in Berlin. It sets no Internet standard.

today: RFC 3026 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a record of 2000-era understandings about ENUM administration in e164.arpa, which relates to RFC 2916.

sections.title: A Liaison From ITU-T to the IETF
sections.content:
Working Party 1/2 of the ITU-T held a meeting of its collaborators in Berlin, Germany, on 19-26 October 2000. Several contributions on the agenda concerned RFC 2916, E.164 Number and DNS from the IETF ENUM Working Group, and how E.164-based resources are administered in the DNS. Several IETF members attended to help with the discussion.

This memo is the resulting liaison: a statement from the working party to the IETF and ISOC that records what the collaborators understood after the talks. It covers only the provision and update of E.164 numerical values in the DNS, not policy or operational functions. It notes that most ENUM service and administrative decisions are national issues under the purview of ITU Member States.
sections.plainLanguage: A group of phone experts met and talked with some Internet experts. This letter writes down what they all agreed on.

sections.title: Zones of an e164.arpa Name
sections.content:
To talk about responsibility, the memo defines three zones using the example name 1.5.1.5.0.2.0.4.1.3.3.e164.arpa (as in RFC 2916):

  • Domain zone: e164.arpa itself.
  • Country code zone: 3.3., which is 1, 2 or 3 digits depending on the country code.
  • National zone: 1.5.1.5.0.2.0.4.1., the rest of the number.

The term administration here means providing and updating the E.164 values that go into the zones of a domain name in the e164.arpa domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone number is read backwards like an address: country first, then the rest. The letter gives each part a name so everyone can say who looks after it.

sections.title: Who Administers What
sections.content:
Administration of the domain zone was agreed to be outside the scope of the meeting and the working party. For the rest:

  • Country code zone: the ITU provides assignment information to DNS administrators and ensures each Member State has authorized including its country code. Spare or test codes normally get no DNS entry. The entity holding a test code supplies its own assignment information.
  • National zone, geographic resources: a national matter, administered by the Member State(s) holding the country code. In an integrated plan such as country code 1, each country may administer its portion differently.
  • National zone, codes shared by networks: the entity the resource is assigned to provides the information.
  • National zone, codes shared by groups of countries: the administrative entity named by the countries of the group provides it. This category depends on approval of draft Recommendation E.164.3.

Each administrative entity is separately responsible for telling DNS administrators about later changes. Assigned geographic numbers that the right entity has not authorized are never entered into the DNS. For example, if a country has not approved ENUM, its numbers are not entered. All parties are to follow the pertinent ITU Recommendations, for example E.164, E.164.1, E.190 and E.195.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a big phone book with sections. The country's section is filled in by the world phone club, each country fills in its own pages, and nobody writes a page the owner has not approved.

sections.title: Number Portability and Service Issues
sections.content:
On number portability, the working party agreed to study it further in the context of ENUM, and understood that the study would not affect the IETF's work. The study will also try to identify options and guidance for those who supply administrative information to DNS administrators. Portability issues are to be addressed in a draft supplement to Recommendation E.370.

Items from the Q.10/2 Rapporteur Group on service issues cover freephone service, widened to include International Premium Rate Service and International Shared Cost Service. Preliminary findings were that routing such a call depends on learning the geographic point of origination, for example the calling number, and that a proxy server would then redirect or forward the call. Choice of the IP gateway in a PSTN-to-IP call flow may depend on options available to telephony carriers.
sections.plainLanguage: There were still open questions, like what happens when you keep your phone number but switch companies. The group said it would keep studying them.

sections.title: Security Considerations Added by the IESG
sections.content:
The IESG added a short security section. ENUM stores its information in the DNS, and delegation and distributed administration follow DNS routines, while E.164 numbers are distributed by a different algorithm than domain names.

If delegation and mapping between E.164 and DNS are not done carefully, there is a risk of napping of E.164 numbers when they are stored in the DNS. It is also important to preserve the strictly hierarchical DNS (see RFC 2826).
sections.plainLanguage: If the two phone books are not lined up carefully, someone could grab a number that belongs to someone else. The DNS also has to stay one tidy tree.

references.text: IAB, "IAB Technical Comment on the Unique DNS Root", RFC 2826, May 2000.
